part_title: Translation, Speech Transcription and Polly Voices
review_basis: Visually inspected all 29 original public/course-visuals/aif-course/module-08 numbered WebP images individually in order. Narration rewritten following exact diagram arrows, visible text/examples, numeric values, callouts, and exam comparisons, with product lifecycle caveats.

scenes.title: Amazon Translate
scenes.narration: Begin with the English product description at top left: Your order is ready. Follow the arrow to Amazon Translate, then the yellow Spanish result Tu pedido está listo, and on to an international website. The far-right yellow panel adds optional human review for important meaning and tone. In the lower worked example the input text enters the Translate API and leaves as Spanish text; nothing in that flow processes an audio file. The service-comparison panel shows three distinct directions: Translate is text to text across languages, Transcribe is speech to text, and Polly is text to spoken audio. Do not substitute them just because all three involve language. At the far right, the multilingual knowledge-base use case shows how translated articles can help customers find answers in their own language. Review culturally sensitive or high-impact wording before publishing. The exam check is to identify what form your input and output actually take.

scenes.title: Amazon Transcribe
scenes.narration: At the upper left, a recorded customer call enters Amazon Transcribe. The next box names automatic speech recognition, A S R, which changes audio into text. Two optional side branches show language identification and personal-information redaction; not every configuration supports every option. The resulting transcript contains timestamps, and the rightmost box shows how an organization can search call archives or create video captions. The lower worked example makes this concrete: the caller says My order is delayed. The transcript displays My order at 00:00:00.000 and is delayed at 00:00:01.250. These example timestamps illustrate the output format, not guaranteed timing for arbitrary recordings. At bottom right compare Transcribe with Polly. Transcribe starts with speech and produces text; Polly starts with text and produces speech. When reviewing quality, listen to sample audio because noise and accents may cause recognition mistakes.

scenes.title: Transcribe – Toxicity Detection
scenes.narration: This five-stage diagram describes moderation of a prerecorded US English support call. Stage one supplies the audio file. Stage two is an Amazon Transcribe batch job with toxicity detection, not a real-time streaming moderation service. Stage three presents a transcript divided into time intervals. The first segment from 00:00 to 00:08 is marked NONE, the middle segment from 00:08 to 00:15 is marked INSULT with high illustrative confidence, and the final segment from 00:15 to 00:27 is marked NONE. Stage four is a human reviewer who considers context and company policy before deciding what action is appropriate. Stage five records that decision without automatically imposing sanctions. The bottom table repeats these three segments and categories. Confidence is not proof of someone's intent, and a segment may require context before enforcement. The exam cue: toxicity detection here means batch audio analysis in US English with human moderation, not universal language support or an autonomous disciplinary system.

scenes.title: Amazon Transcribe – Improving Accuracy
scenes.narration: Use the actual example at the upper left: the audio contains the specialist phrase AsterValve inspection. A baseline recognizer might transcribe it as a star valve inspection. The orange custom vocabulary box teaches exact Phrase entries and optional DisplayAs formatting, while the purple custom language model learns domain phrasing from manuals, inspection reports and other text. The right-hand result shows a more accurate transcription as an illustration; actual accuracy must be measured rather than guaranteed. At the bottom compare four paths: baseline recognition, vocabulary-only with AsterValve added as a phrase, domain language-model training, and a supported combination of both. The caution in the top orange box is important: the old IPA and SoundsLike vocabulary pronunciation fields are ignored by current documentation. Choose custom vocabulary for a small known list of product names, and domain text training for broader industry language. Evaluate results on representative audio before declaring success.

scenes.title: Amazon Polly
scenes.narration: Read the four boxes across the top. An application sends the text Your package is ready into Amazon Polly. Polly synthesizes natural-sounding speech and returns audio, such as an MP3 file. The final box is a phone, website or accessibility feature that plays the notification aloud. In the lower-left worked example the same sentence moves through three steps: the application sends text, Polly synthesizes speech, and the user hears an audio notification. The four numbered steps on the lower middle add a configuration detail: choose a supported language and voice, request synthesis, then play the resulting file. The right-hand exam panel warns what Polly does not do. Polly is not an intent manager or a text translator; Transcribe converts speech into text. When asked for spoken output from text, Polly is the correct service. For a real product, verify supported voices and pronunciation of important names.

scenes.title: Polly – Advanced Features
scenes.narration: Start with the input Welcome to AWS on the left. The gold lexicon panel can tell Polly how to pronounce AWS, for example as Amazon Web Services. The purple S S M L panel allows supported delivery instructions such as a spoken pause. Then choose a compatible voice and send the request to Amazon Polly. The upper-right area deliberately separates two outputs: A is an audio file from a synthesis request, while B is speech-mark data, such as word timings, from a separate request. They are not the same output format. The lower reading-app example requests audio, requests speech marks separately, and then uses word timing to highlight Welcome while the recording plays. The exam summary distinguishes lexicon for pronunciation, S S M L for delivery, and speech marks for timing. Support varies by voice and engine; the generative engine does not support speech marks under the documented constraints.
